211.title: Pauri 29, sound: bhugat giaan
211.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite Japji Sahib every morning as part of Nitnem; pauris 28 to 31 are often heard as Guru Nanak answering the Nath yogis in their own vocabulary, and each ends with the refrain aades tisai aades.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pauri 28, where the yogi's earrings became contentment, and your line: conquer the mind. Today, the next stanza for the yogis, sound first.

Mealtime in a yogi camp. The one who keeps the stores walks down the line, handing out the shared food, and somebody blows a small horn; the note hangs in the evening air. Commentators say the yogis had their own word for that meal: bhugat. Sikh tradition remembers Guru Nanak meeting and talking with yogis on his travels. Yesterday he took their earrings and their ash and turned them inward. Today he sits down at their dinner, and the first line of Pauri 29 is built from what's on the table.
screen: `MEALTIME IN A YOGI CAMP.` → `THE SHARED MEAL, BHUGAT.` → `NANAK SITS DOWN TO EAT.`

segments.voice: Here is the first line of Pauri 29, as Guru Nanak sang it: bhugat giaan daiaa bhanddaaran, ghatt ghatt vaajeh naad. One word at a time. Bhugat: the meal handed out in the yogis' gathering. Giaan: wisdom, knowing. So bhugat giaan: let wisdom be the meal. Daiaa: compassion. Bhanddaaran: the one who keeps the storeroom and serves from it. The word even has a feminine ending, the woman of the stores. So compassion is the one holding the ladle. Then the second half changes its sound. Ghatt ghatt vaajeh naad. A ghatt is a clay pot, and in the Granth it often means the body, or the heart inside it. Ghatt ghatt: in every pot, in every heart. Vaajeh: they play, they ring. Naad: the note, the sound, the same word the yogis used for the call of their horn. In every heart, the note is sounding. Now hear how the line is built. The first half is four solid words, set down like dishes on a cloth: bhugat, giaan, daiaa, bhanddaaran. The second half doubles a word, ghatt ghatt, then rings out on naad, the way a horn might close a meal. And like the stanzas around it, this one ends with a refrain taken from the yogis' own greeting: aades tisai aades, my salute to Him, my salute. The whole meaning comes tomorrow. Today, just the sound, and the two words that start it: bhugat giaan.
screen: `BHUGAT GIAAN — WISDOM IS THE MEAL.` · `DAIAA BHANDDAARAN — COMPASSION SERVES.` · `GHATT GHATT VAAJEH NAAD.` · `A LINE BUILT LIKE A MEAL.` · then, large: `BHUGAT GIAAN.`

segments.voice: Say the first line aloud three times, slowly: bhugat giaan daiaa bhanddaaran, ghatt ghatt vaajeh naad, the first half steady in four even steps, the second half ringing. Then stop, and listen for whatever is still sounding in you after the words end. When a thought wanders in, come back by whispering ghatt ghatt, in every heart.
Naad, the note, the sound. The stanza where Guru Nanak sits down at the yogis' meal: wisdom is the food, compassion serves it, and a note sounds in every heart.
Your line: bhugat giaan. A whole line, set out like a meal. That's day two hundred eleven.

212.title: Pauri 29, meaning: wisdom for food
212.hook: let wisdom be your food and compassion the one who serves it; the music sounds in every heart (Japji 29)
212.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite Japji Sahib each morning; in the gurdwara's langar, people still sit in rows and are served by volunteers with a ladle, which many hear as a living picture of compassion serving the meal.

segments.voice: Yesterday, naad, the note in every heart, and your line, bhugat giaan: wisdom is the meal. Today, what the whole stanza means.

A school cook slips an extra scoop onto a tray because the kid in front of her looks like they've had a rough morning. A grandmother won't sit down until every plate is full. An uncle at a wedding keeps coming back with the tray. Years later, it can be the hands that stay in memory, more than the food. The same rice tastes different handed over by someone who wants you fed. In a gurdwara's langar, people sit in rows, and volunteers come down the line with a bucket and a ladle. Pauri 29 puts a server like that at the center of its meal.
screen: `THE EXTRA SCOOP.` → `THE HANDS STAY IN MEMORY.` → `THE LADLE IN LANGAR.`

segments.voice: Guru Nanak is speaking to yogis, in their own camp words. Their shared meal was bhugat, so he says: let wisdom be your bhugat. Not a rule, not a diet. What actually feeds you is understanding. Then he names the server: daiaa bhanddaaran, compassion is the keeper of the stores. Wisdom without compassion is a locked pantry: someone knows a great deal and hands none of it out, or hands it out with a sneer. In Pauri 29, wisdom is only a meal when compassion holds the ladle. Then the horn. The yogis blew a horn to sound the naad, the note they listened for in meditation. Nanak says: ghatt ghatt vaajeh naad. It's already sounding, in every heart. No horn needed. The yogis honored their great teachers as Naths, masters. Nanak says the One is the true Nath, holding every creature on His string. And the miraculous powers some yogis worked for, riddhi and siddhi? Nanak calls them avaraa saad, other flavors. Tasty, maybe, but not the meal. Then a wide line: sanjog vijog, meeting and parting, both keep the world turning, and each of us receives our share as it is written. And the refrain, the yogis' own greeting turned toward God: aades tisai aades, my salute to Him. So the menu is short. Wisdom to eat, compassion to serve it, and a note already playing in you.
screen: `WISDOM IS THE MEAL.` · `COMPASSION HOLDS THE LADLE.` · `THE NOTE IS ALREADY PLAYING.` · `POWERS ARE JUST OTHER FLAVORS.` · then, large: `COMPASSION SERVES THE FOOD.`

segments.voice: If you have something to eat or drink nearby, take one slow bite or sip; if not, picture your next meal. As you taste it, think of one thing you understand now that you didn't a year ago, and who handed it to you: a teacher, a parent, a friend, a stranger. Then rest, breathing, and listen for the note Nanak says is already sounding.
Nath, master, the yogis' name for their teacher. Wisdom as the meal, compassion as the one who serves it, a note in every heart, and miraculous powers called nothing more than other flavors.
Your line: compassion serves the food. Powers are side dishes; wisdom is the meal. Day two hundred twelve, done.

213.title: Pauri 30, sound: ekaa maaee
213.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite Japji Sahib each morning; Pauri 30 is one of four stanzas addressed to the Nath yogis, and like the others it closes with the refrain aades tisai aades and aad aneel anaad anaahat, jug jug eko ves.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nath, the true master, and your line: compassion serves the food. Today, a new stanza, and it opens like a story.

Plenty of languages have a way of starting a story so the listener knows one is coming. Once upon a time. Long, long ago. In the beginning. A child hears those words and settles in, even before anything has happened. The sound itself says: listen, this is how things came to be. Pauri 30 of Japji opens with that kind of sound. Four words, two pairs, and the pairs rhyme, so it lands in the ear like the first line of a very old tale. It's still part of Guru Nanak's answer to the yogis, and it takes a picture they already knew.
screen: `ONCE UPON A TIME.` → `A SOUND THAT SAYS, LISTEN.` → `FOUR WORDS, TWO RHYMES.`

segments.voice: Here is how Pauri 30 begins: ekaa maaee jugat viaaee, tin chele paravaan. The first pair. Ekaa: one, a single. Maaee: mother. Ekaa maaee: one mother; hear how the two words lean on the long aa. Then the second pair. Jugat: a way, a method, and also a joining; commentators note it was also a yogi word for technique. Viaaee: gave birth, brought forth. So: by a certain joining, she gave birth. Now the rhyme: maaee, viaaee. The line swings like a cradle. Then three more words: tin chele paravaan. Tin: three. Chele: disciples, students, the same word used for a guru's followers. Paravaan: accepted, approved. One mother, by a joining, brought forth three approved disciples. Who is this one mother? Commentators answer in different ways. Some read her as maya, the power that makes the visible world. Others hear the Creator's own creative power. Tomorrow, that, and who the three are. At the end of the stanza, the refrain returns in full: aad aneel anaad anaahat, jug jug eko ves. The first, the pure, without beginning, unbroken, one form through every age. It closed pauris 28 and 29 too. Notice how it answers today's opening. The story starts with a birth. The refrain reminds you who was never born.
screen: `EKAA MAAEE — ONE MOTHER.` · `JUGAT VIAAEE — BY A JOINING, A BIRTH.` · `TIN CHELE PARAVAAN — THREE DISCIPLES.` · `JUG JUG EKO VES — ONE THROUGH EVERY AGE.` · then, large: `EKAA MAAEE.`

segments.voice: Say the first line aloud, slowly, three times: ekaa maaee jugat viaaee, tin chele paravaan, letting the rhyme rock, maaee, viaaee, like something you'd say to a child at night. Then stay quiet: breathe in and silently think ekaa, one; breathe out and think maaee, mother. If your mind drifts, the rhyme will bring you back.
Chele, disciples, students. It opens like an ancient tale: one mother, by a joining, gave birth to three approved disciples.
Your line: ekaa maaee. Four words that rock gently, like a cradle. See you tomorrow.

214.title: Pauri 30, meaning: He sees, unseen
214.hook: the old picture of three powers that make, keep and end the world; all act by His order, and He sees them though they do not see Him (Japji 30)
214.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite Japji Sahib each morning; Pauri 30 is commonly explained as placing every power, however great, within the one divine order, and its closing line, He sees them though they do not see Him, is often read as a picture of the Creator's care.

segments.voice: Yesterday, chele, disciples, and your line, ekaa maaee: one mother, by a joining, brought forth three. Today, who the three are, and the One who sees them.

A small kid on a climbing frame, deep in some game only they understand. On a bench at the edge of the playground, a parent is watching. The kid never looks over. Doesn't need to. They climb higher and braver, because someone has an eye on them. Put a stranger on that same bench, and the same watching means something else. Being seen can be a threat or a blessing. It depends on who's looking, and how. Pauri 30 ends with someone who sees and is not seen.
screen: `A KID ON THE CLIMBING FRAME.` → `A PARENT ON THE BENCH.` → `WHO'S LOOKING, AND HOW?`

segments.voice: The stanza names the three disciples. Ik sansaaree: one who brings forth the world. Ik bhanddaaree: one who keeps the stores, who sustains. Ik laae deebaan: one who holds court, who judges and brings things to an end. Commentators connect these three with a picture from Hindu tradition that Guru Nanak's hearers knew well: Brahma who creates, Vishnu who preserves, and Shiva who ends and transforms. Nanak doesn't argue with the picture. He places it. Next line: jiv tis bhaavai tivai chalaavai, jiv hovai furmaan. As it pleases Him, so He makes them move, as His order is. Furmaan: a command, the word for a royal decree. Even the greatest powers people could imagine work within the one order, the hukam from Pauri 1. Then the turn, the heart of the stanza: oh vekhai onaa nadar na aavai. He sees them, but He does not come into their sight. And Nanak adds: bahutaa eh viddaan. This is the great wonder. Not a warning. A wonder. Sikh teachers hear this seeing as care, the way the Granth elsewhere speaks of the Creator making and then watching over what was made. The One who can't be seen is not a stranger on the bench. More like the parent: the eye that lets you play.

segments.voice: Remember a time you felt seen kindly: a teacher who noticed you, a friend who knew what was wrong before you said it, a grandparent watching you with pride. Sit inside that memory as if that kind attention were still on you, here, right now; you don't need to look back at it. Breathe, and let yourself be seen.
Viddaan, wonder. Three powers that make, keep and end the world, all moving by one order; and the One sees them, though they cannot see Him. This is the great wonder.
Your line: seen, though unseen. Even the greatest powers move inside one order. That's day two hundred fourteen.

215.title: Pauri 31: storehouses everywhere
215.hook: aasan loe loe: His seat and storehouses are in every world, filled once and for all (Japji 31)
215.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite Japji Sahib each morning; Pauri 31 closes the four stanzas addressed to the Nath yogis, and its picture of storehouses in every world is often recalled as a teaching on trust and contentment.

segments.voice: Yesterday: viddaan, wonder, and your line, seen, though unseen. Today, the last of the four stanzas for the yogis.

You've seen the photos: grocery shelves stripped bare because everyone got scared at the same time. Toilet paper gone, bread gone, one sad can of beans. Fear of running out makes people grab. Now cut open one apple and count the seeds. Five, maybe eight. Each could grow a tree, and each tree could drop hundreds of apples a year for decades. One apple holds an orchard. The world is stocked in a way that's hard to take in, and most days it goes unnoticed behind the worry about the shelves. Pauri 31 is about the storehouses.
screen: `EMPTY SHELVES.` → `ONE APPLE, EIGHT SEEDS.` → `AN ORCHARD INSIDE.`

segments.voice: Pauri 31 is short, and it opens with a yogi's word. Aasan loe loe bhanddaar. Aasan is a seat, the mat or skin a yogi carried and sat on to meditate. Wherever he went, his aasan went too, and that spot became his place. Guru Nanak says the One's aasan is loe loe, in world after world. There's no single spot to travel to. Bhanddaar: storehouses. In Pauri 29, compassion was the bhanddaaran, the keeper of the stores. In Pauri 30, one of the three powers was the bhanddaaree, the one who sustains. Now the storehouses themselves are in every world. Then today's line: jo kichh paaiaa su ekaa vaar. Whatever was put in, was put in once. Commentators read it as a creation already provided for: the stores filled at the start, not in a panic every morning. Kar kar vekhai sirjanhaar: having made it, the Creator watches over it, the same care as yesterday. Sache kee saachee kaar: true is the work of the True One. And the refrain, one last time: aades tisai aades, my salute to Him. With that, Nanak's answer to the yogis is complete. Their earrings, their meal, their horn, their seat: each one turned toward the One who is everywhere. Tomorrow, the Japji starts to climb.

segments.voice: Look at one place you can see or picture, a window with a tree in it, a kitchen shelf, your own hands, as a storehouse: leaves, light, grain, breath, years of work in your fingers. Don't count what's missing; notice what's already there, and let it be more than you expected. Then breathe, one easy breath after another, drawing from a store you didn't fill.

216.title: Pauri 32, sound: ik doo jeebhau
216.tomorrow: Pauri 32, meaning: the steps of the ladder
216.howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite Japji Sahib each morning; Pauri 32 opens the stretch many teachers call the ladder and the realms, and it opens with the image of a single tongue multiplied into two million.

segments.voice: Yesterday: aasan, the yogi's seat, and your line, filled once, for all. Today, a new part of the Japji begins.

Listen to a small child tell a parent how much they love them. I love you a hundred. No, a thousand. A million, a billion, infinity. Infinity plus one. The numbers climb because the feeling is bigger than any number they know. Grown-ups smile, but the child has found something true: when love runs past what you can say, you reach for the biggest counting word there is, and then go past it. Guru Nanak does something like this in Pauri 32, with a tongue instead of a number. It opens a new stretch of Japji, the ladder and the realms. Today, how it sounds.
screen: `I LOVE YOU A MILLION.` → `INFINITY PLUS ONE.` → `A TONGUE INSTEAD OF A NUMBER.`

segments.voice: Here is the opening: ik doo jeebhau lakh hohi, lakh hoveh lakh vees. Ik: one. Doo: from, out of. Jeebhau: tongue. So, from one tongue. Lakh: a hundred thousand; in South Asia people still count in lakhs, the way Americans count in thousands. Hohi: become. From one tongue, let there be a hundred thousand. Then Nanak goes past it: lakh hoveh lakh vees, let those hundred thousand become twenty times a hundred thousand. That's two million tongues, the child's infinity plus one in a poet's language. Now listen. Ik doo jeebhau: three light steps, then a vowel that opens, jee-bhau. Lakh hohi: short and hard. Then lakh hoveh lakh vees, lakh sounding twice like a drumbeat getting faster. You can hear the numbers pile up. What will all those tongues do? That's tomorrow, along with a word that tells you where this stanza is going. For today, notice the wish. It isn't for more money, or more time, or more of anything for oneself. It's a wish for more ways to say one thing.

segments.voice: Say the first line aloud three times, slowly, letting each lakh land like a drumbeat: ik doo jeebhau lakh hohi, lakh hoveh lakh vees. Then close your mouth and let your one tongue rest, soft, behind your teeth, doing nothing. Breathe through your nose, and let any thought pass without saying it.
Lakh, a hundred thousand. It opens with a wish: from one tongue, a hundred thousand, and then two million. The first stanza of the ladder.
Your line: ik doo jeebhau, from one tongue. The next stanzas climb from this wish. See you tomorrow.

217.title: Pauri 32, meaning: the steps of the ladder
217.hook: if one tongue became a hundred thousand, I would repeat the Name on each; these are the steps to the Lord (Japji 32)
217.howItsDone: Sikhs repeat Waheguru in simran, sometimes counting on the fingers or on a mala; Pauri 32 pictures repetition of the Name as a staircase, with the arrival given by grace.

segments.voice: Yesterday: lakh, and your line, ik doo jeebhau, from one tongue. That ends a week: wisdom as the meal, with compassion serving; one mother, three powers, and the One seen though unseen; the storehouses, filled once, for all, the end of Nanak's answer to the yogis. Today, what all those tongues would do.

A long staircase. A stadium, an old tower, a subway exit when the escalator's broken. Nobody takes it in one leap. You look at the next step, and the next, and somewhere in the middle you stop counting. Pauri 32 has a staircase too, and it starts on a tongue.
screen: `A LONG STAIRCASE.` → `NOBODY TAKES IT IN ONE LEAP.` → `THE NEXT STEP, AND THE NEXT.`

segments.voice: One tongue became two million. Here's what they'd do. Lakh lakh gerraa aakheeah, ek naam jagdees. With each tongue, round after round, a hundred thousand times, I would say the one Name of the Lord of the world. Gerraa is a round, like one turn of a wheel. Then: et raah pat pavarreeaa, charreeai hoe ikees. On this path are the steps to the Beloved; climbing them, one becomes one with Him. Pavarreeaa, steps. Listen closely and you can hear pauri in it, the name every stanza of Japji carries: a stair, a rung of a ladder. The Japji is built out of steps. But Nanak doesn't let the climb go to anyone's head. Sun galaa aakaas kee, keettaa aaee rees: hearing talk of the heavens, even worms want to copy it. It's a sharp picture of borrowed spiritual talk, people who speak of the top without taking the stairs. And the last line turns everything: Nanak nadaree paaeeai, koorree koorrai tthees. By grace it is reached; the boasting of the false is false. Sikh teachers hold the two halves together. The repeating, round after round, is real effort, a real staircase. The arrival is a gift, the glance of grace.
screen: `A NAME REPEATED, ROUND AFTER ROUND.` · `PAVARREEAA — THE STEPS, LIKE PAURI.` · `EVEN WORMS COPY TALK OF HEAVEN.` · `CLIMB, BUT GRACE BRINGS YOU THERE.` · then, large: `STEP BY STEP.`

segments.voice: In simran, Sikhs repeat Waheguru, a name for the Wondrous Lord; if you'd like, say it twenty times, softly, one finger and one step for each, with no race to the top. If that word isn't yours, count twenty slow breaths instead, each one a step. At twenty, stop climbing, and just stand on that step and rest, breathing.
Pavarreeaa, the steps. One Name repeated on a million tongues: these are the steps to the Beloved. The word echoes pauri itself, and arriving is by grace.
Your line: step by step. You climb, and you don't brag about the top. That's day two hundred seventeen.
